meta.title: Microservices Architecture Guide
meta.description: A practical guide to microservices architecture: service boundaries, communication, data ownership, reliability, observability, security, testing, deployment, and operations.

hero.title: Build services that can change without breaking the system.
hero.description: A decision-first guide to dividing a product into services, owning data, surviving partial failure, and operating the result when the network becomes part of every feature.

sections.title: The microservices mental model
sections.summary: Microservices are independently changeable business capabilities connected by a network, not merely a monolith split into many repositories.

blocks.title: Start with the organisational problem
paragraphs: A microservice architecture is useful when teams need to change different parts of a large product independently. The goal is not to maximise the number of deployables. The goal is to reduce coordination around well-understood business capabilities.

A modular monolith is usually the safer beginning. It keeps calls local, transactions straightforward, and debugging in one process. Move to services when ownership, scaling, isolation, or release cadence creates a measurable constraint—not because a diagram with many boxes looks mature.
blocks.note: If one team owns the whole system and deploys it together, separate processes may add cost without providing independence.

blocks.title: What makes a service genuinely independent
paragraphs: A useful service owns a coherent capability, its implementation, and the data needed to make its decisions. Other services depend on a published contract rather than reaching into its tables or internal modules.

Independent deployment does not mean careless deployment. Contracts still need compatibility, telemetry, and a migration story. Independence means a service can evolve safely without requiring a coordinated release of every consumer.
list: Independent build, test, deployment, and rollback

blocks.title: The distributed-systems tax
paragraphs: A function call becomes a network request that can be slow, duplicated, reordered, or unavailable. A database transaction becomes a workflow across independently failing components. Logs scatter across processes. Local development needs more infrastructure.

Budget for service discovery, authentication, retries, timeouts, tracing, deployment automation, schema evolution, and on-call ownership. These are not optional platform polish; they are part of the architecture.

blocks.title: From product request to service response
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Client] --> B[Edge / gateway]
    B --> C[Owning service]
    C --> D[(Service database)]
    C --> E[Event broker]
    E --> F[Downstream service]
    C --> G[Telemetry]

blocks.title: A practical adoption test
list: Can you name the capability without mentioning a technical layer?
Can one team own its behaviour and production health?
Does independent scaling or delivery solve a current problem?
Can its contract remain smaller and more stable than its internals?
Can you operate it when dependencies are unavailable?
blocks.note: A ‘no’ is a signal to improve modularity first, not a failure to be modern.

sections.title: Finding service boundaries
sections.summary: Good boundaries follow business decisions and change patterns; poor boundaries mirror database tables, UI screens, or organisational history.

blocks.title: Model capabilities, not nouns
paragraphs: An Order service is not valuable because an orders table exists. It is valuable when order placement, pricing commitments, status transitions, and cancellation rules form a cohesive decision-making unit.

Use domain language with product specialists. Look for rules that change together, terms with precise meanings, and workflows with a clear owner. Domain-driven design calls these bounded contexts; the practical point is to stop one model from pretending to mean the same thing everywhere.

blocks.title: Use change coupling as evidence
paragraphs: Study recent work. Files, tables, and teams that repeatedly change together probably belong together. A proposed boundary that forces most features to cross three services is fighting the product rather than separating it.

Runtime calls are only one form of coupling. Shared releases, shared databases, synchronized schema changes, and a central team approving every modification can produce a distributed monolith even when each box has its own deployment.
list: Few synchronous calls on common paths
A contract expressed in domain language

blocks.title: Extract with a strangler path
paragraphs: Choose one capability with a clear seam. Route new behaviour to the new service while the old application continues serving everything else. Move authority deliberately, observe production behaviour, and remove the old path only after consumers have migrated.
Avoid copying a table and declaring both copies authoritative. During migration, define which system accepts writes and how other representations catch up.

blocks.title: Map ownership before APIs
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Checkout capability] --> B[Order service]
    B --> C[(Orders)]
    B --> D[Payment contract]
    D --> E[Payment service]
    E --> F[(Payments)]
    B --> G[Fulfilment event]
    G --> H[Fulfilment service]

blocks.title: Recognise boundaries that are too small
paragraphs: If two services always deploy together, share every incident, and cannot answer a request without each other, the split has not created autonomy. Merge them or move the boundary until each side owns a useful outcome.
A service per entity, CRUD endpoint, or engineer maximises operational surface while preserving the original coupling. Prefer fewer, richer services.

sections.title: Communication patterns
sections.summary: Choose synchronous calls for immediate answers and asynchronous messages for decoupled workflows, while designing every boundary for latency and failure.

blocks.title: Use synchronous calls when the caller needs the answer now
paragraphs: HTTP or RPC is appropriate for queries, validation that must complete before a response, and commands whose immediate result matters. Keep call chains short: every hop adds latency and another way for the request to fail.
Set explicit deadlines. A default client timeout is rarely a product decision. Propagate cancellation and include correlation identifiers so one request can be followed across services.

blocks.title: Use events to announce completed facts
paragraphs: An event says something already happened: OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured, or ProfileUpdated. Consumers decide independently what to do. This reduces temporal coupling because the producer does not need every consumer online.

Events should carry stable identifiers, occurrence time, schema version, and enough context for consumers to act without repeatedly calling the producer. Do not put secrets into a broadly distributed event.

blocks.title: Assume messages can arrive more than once
paragraphs: Most practical brokers provide at-least-once delivery. A consumer may finish its work and crash before acknowledging the message, causing redelivery. Make handlers idempotent with a processed-message record, a naturally idempotent write, or a business key.
Ordering is normally local to a partition or entity key, not global. Design state transitions so stale events are rejected or safely ignored.

blocks.title: Publish reliably with an outbox
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Command] --> B[Service transaction]
    B --> C[(Domain data)]
    B --> D[(Outbox row)]
    D --> E[Publisher]
    E --> F[Message broker]
    F --> G[Idempotent consumer]

blocks.title: Treat contracts as products
paragraphs: Document semantics, not only field types. State whether absence differs from null, whether amounts are minor units, which errors are retryable, and what compatibility consumers can expect.
Use consumer-driven contract tests where they help, but keep ownership clear: a producer must not become unable to improve because consumers assert accidental implementation details.

sections.title: Data ownership and consistency
sections.summary: Each service should own its source of truth; cross-service workflows then require explicit consistency, duplication, and recovery choices.

blocks.title: Do not share writable tables
paragraphs: A private database prevents another service from bypassing rules and coupling itself to storage details. Database-per-service is a logical ownership rule; services may share infrastructure when isolation, permissions, backups, and operational needs permit it.

Consumers obtain data through a contract or maintain a local projection from events. Duplication is deliberate in distributed systems because autonomy is often more valuable than a perfectly normalised global schema.

blocks.title: Name the consistency the product needs
paragraphs: Strong consistency is appropriate inside a service transaction. Across services, eventual consistency is common: changes become visible after propagation. Translate that technical fact into product behaviour, such as showing ‘payment processing’ rather than claiming completion prematurely.
Not every field deserves immediate propagation. Inventory reservation may be urgent; an analytics dashboard can lag. State acceptable staleness per use case.

blocks.title: Coordinate long-running work with a saga
paragraphs: A saga is a sequence of local transactions. Choreography lets services react to events; orchestration gives one workflow component responsibility for the next command. Neither creates a distributed ACID transaction.
Define compensating actions before implementation. A refund is not literally an undo of a captured payment—it is a new auditable business action that can also fail.

blocks.title: Make partial progress visible
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Create order] --> B[Reserve inventory]
    B --> C[Capture payment]
    C --> D[Confirm order]
    C --> E[Payment failed]
    E --> F[Release inventory]
    F --> G[Cancel order]

blocks.title: Evolve data without stopping consumers
paragraphs: Use expand-and-contract changes: add the new representation, make producers and consumers compatible, migrate data, switch reads and writes, then remove the old shape. Deployments between those steps must remain safe.
For events, prefer additive changes and tolerant readers. A schema registry can enforce compatibility, but teams still need semantic discipline.

sections.title: Reliability and failure
sections.summary: Production microservices must expect partial failure and prevent one unhealthy dependency from consuming the entire system.

blocks.title: Design for partial failure
paragraphs: A dependency can be slow while everything else is healthy. Threads, connections, and request queues can fill before an outright error appears. Track saturation and latency, not only success rates.
Decide what the product should do when each dependency is unavailable: reject safely, serve stale data, queue work, remove an optional feature, or ask the user to retry.

blocks.title: Timeout first, then retry carefully
paragraphs: A retry without a timeout simply waits longer. Use a deadline based on the caller’s remaining budget. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, and cap both attempts and total elapsed time.
Retries multiply load during an incident. Never blindly retry non-idempotent work. Carry an idempotency key when a command may be repeated.

blocks.title: Contain damage with isolation
paragraphs: Circuit breakers stop repeatedly calling a known-unhealthy dependency. Bulkheads reserve resources so one dependency cannot exhaust every worker or connection. Rate limits protect both your system and downstream services.
These mechanisms need observable states and conservative recovery. A circuit that flaps open and closed can be more disruptive than a clear degraded mode.

blocks.title: Follow the latency budget
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[900 ms request budget] --> B[Gateway 50 ms]
    B --> C[Service 250 ms]
    C --> D[Dependency 350 ms]
    D --> E[Response reserve 250 ms]

blocks.title: Use SLOs to choose engineering work
paragraphs: An SLI measures user-visible behaviour such as successful requests under a latency threshold. An SLO states the target. The error budget is the permitted unreliability over a period.
When a service burns its budget quickly, reduce change and repair reliability. When it remains comfortably healthy, the team can invest more aggressively in product delivery.

sections.title: Observability, delivery, and security
sections.summary: A service is not complete until teams can deploy it safely, trace its behaviour, protect its boundaries, and own incidents.

blocks.title: Correlate logs, metrics, and traces
paragraphs: Metrics reveal trends and alert conditions. Logs explain discrete events. Distributed traces show where time and errors travel through a request. Use the same service name, environment, trace identifier, and deployment version across all three.
Instrument boundaries first: inbound requests, outbound calls, broker publishing and consumption, database queries, and important business outcomes.

blocks.title: Make deployments boring and reversible
paragraphs: Build immutable artifacts once and promote the same artifact between environments. Automate health checks, progressive rollout, rollback, and database compatibility checks.

A deployment is not successful because containers started. It is successful when user-facing indicators remain healthy. Compare the new version against the previous one during canary or gradual traffic shifts.

blocks.title: Authenticate identity and authorise every operation
paragraphs: A trusted network is not sufficient. Validate service identity, user context, audience, expiry, and permission at the service performing the action. Keep credentials short-lived and rotate them automatically.
Minimise sensitive data in APIs, events, logs, and traces. Encrypt transport, isolate secrets from images and source control, and audit privileged actions.

blocks.title: Give every service a production owner
list: Dashboard and alerts tied to an SLO

blocks.title: Earn complexity gradually
paragraphs: Standardise common concerns through a small platform: service templates, identity, telemetry, deployment, and local tooling. Keep the paved road helpful rather than mandatory bureaucracy.
Regularly remove services whose boundary no longer pays for itself. Architecture is a living trade-off, not a one-way journey toward more boxes.
blocks.note: The healthiest microservice estate may become smaller as teams learn where the real boundaries are.
